title: Eat Widely, Vote Wisely: Lessons from a Campaign Against Vote Buying in Uganda

reviewed_pages.printed_pages: unnumbered title page and 1–33, followed by References
reviewed_pages.excluded_pages: PDF 38–66, explicitly labeled Appendix (For Online Publication)

boundary_evidence.paraphrase: PDF page 38 begins a separately labeled online-publication appendix; review therefore covers PDF pages 1–37 and excludes pages 38–66.

source_scope: Published/author main article only: PDF pages 1–37, including main-text tables, figures, notes, and footnotes. PDF pages 38–66 online-publication appendix and all external materials were excluded.

experiments.name: ACFIM randomized-saturation anti-vote-buying field experiment
experiments.classification_rationale: Primary experiment: the article's central causal design randomly assigns parishes to saturation arms and eligible polling stations/villages within partial-saturation parishes; all survey, electoral, and policy follow-ups reuse this assignment.

design_map.label: Target population
design_map.value: Registered voters and polling-station communities in 918 Ugandan parishes with pre-existing ACFIM presence; broader population target NR.

evidence.anchor: Our baseline sample included 918 parishes with some ACFIM presence
evidence.paraphrase: The experimental frame was 918 parishes with pre-intervention ACFIM presence.

evidence.anchor: the ACFIM intervention could only take place in villages where a local ACFIM activist resided or was well known
evidence.paraphrase: Eligible villages required a resident or locally known ACFIM activist; eligible polling stations served at least one such village.

design_map.label: Eligibility criteria
design_map.value: Parish had some prior ACFIM presence; eligible villages had a resident/known activist; eligible stations served ≥1 eligible village; survey respondents were registered, age 18+, and village residents.

evidence.anchor: the ACFIM intervention could only take place in villages where a local ACFIM activist resided or was well known
evidence.paraphrase: Eligible villages required a resident or locally known ACFIM activist; eligible polling stations served at least one such village.

evidence.anchor: randomly sampled from the official voter register in each village
evidence.paraphrase: Endline respondents were sampled from voter registers, stratified by age category and gender; they had to be registered, age 18+, and village residents.

design_map.label: Recruitment procedure
design_map.value: Parish/sample-frame recruitment into the 918-parish study is NR. Endline voters were randomly sampled from official registers within villages, stratified by age category and gender.

evidence.anchor: randomly sampled from the official voter register in each village
evidence.paraphrase: Endline respondents were sampled from voter registers, stratified by age category and gender; they had to be registered, age 18+, and village residents.
The main article does not explain how the 918 parishes/53 districts entered the study beyond requiring ACFIM presence.

design_map.label: Field dates and setting
design_map.value: Uganda; intervention in the final three weeks before the February 2016 general election; voter surveys March 2–July 19, 2016; later administrative outcomes in 2016–17 and 2021.

evidence.anchor: The surveys started on March 2, 2016, and ended on July 19, 2016
evidence.paraphrase: The intervention occurred in Uganda during the final three weeks before the February 2016 election; endline survey dates were March 2–July 19, 2016.

design_map.label: Number recruited and analyzed
design_map.value: 918 parishes; 2,796 eligible villages served by 1,603 eligible polling stations; survey N=28,454. Number approached/recruited and full arm-by-arm flow NR. Table Ns range by outcome.

evidence.anchor: Our baseline sample included 918 parishes with some ACFIM presence
evidence.paraphrase: The experimental frame was 918 parishes with pre-intervention ACFIM presence.

evidence.anchor: endline survey of 28,454 registered voters
evidence.paraphrase: The article reports 28,454 surveyed registered voters, electoral records, and test-score matching; it does not report the number approached for the survey.

evidence.anchor: 1,585 of the 1,603 (99%) polling stations
evidence.paraphrase: 2016 electoral data matched 1,585 of 1,603 experimental-sample polling stations; the reason for 1% loss is stated in footnote 8.

evidence.anchor: we can assign test scores to 2,052 polling stations in 695 parishes
evidence.paraphrase: Test scores were matched for 2,052 polling stations; footnote 12 identifies spatial-data and score-data losses.

design_map.label: Experimental arms or randomized attributes
design_map.value: Parish arms: pure control, partial saturation, high saturation. Station/village statuses: directly treated, untreated spillover in treated parishes, and pure control. No randomized attributes (ordinary bundled intervention).

evidence.anchor: three roughly equally-sized groups: a pure control group, a partial-saturation treatment group, and a high-saturation group
evidence.paraphrase: Parishes were assigned to pure control, partial saturation, or high saturation; eligible stations in partial parishes were split between direct treatment and spillover.

design_map.label: Unit of randomization
design_map.value: Parish at stage 1; eligible polling station plus corresponding villages at stage 2 within partial-saturation parishes.

evidence.anchor: two levels of randomization
evidence.paraphrase: Randomization occurred first at parish level and then at eligible polling-station level (with corresponding villages) within partial-saturation parishes.

design_map.label: Allocation probabilities and restrictions
design_map.value: Parish groups roughly equal (exact probabilities/counts NR); half of eligible stations treated in partial parishes; lone eligible station 50%; all eligible stations treated in high saturation; stratified parish allocation; no station split.

evidence.anchor: half of the eligible polling stations were allocated to treatment
evidence.paraphrase: Parish groups were only described as roughly equal. Within partial-saturation parishes, half of eligible stations were treated; a sole eligible station had 50% probability. High-saturation parishes treated all eligible stations.

evidence.anchor: stratified along baseline measures of ACFIM eligibility ... voter population; and support for the incumbent
evidence.paraphrase: Parish assignment was stratified by the three-way interaction of quartiles of ACFIM presence, voter population, and district-level 2011 NRM support; stations were not split.

design_map.label: Exact treatment and comparator
design_map.value: Bundled ACFIM anti-vote-buying campaign versus no direct campaign (pure controls and spillover comparisons). Exact meeting scripts, poster text, and complete language-specific materials NR.

evidence.anchor: leaflets, village meetings, and robocalls
evidence.paraphrase: The bundle included household leaflets, three structured village meetings, resolutions/posters where adopted, and an eve-of-election automated call. The main article gives the call verbatim but not all scripts, poster text, or language-specific materials.

design_map.label: Outcome definitions and timing
design_map.value: Survey belief/resolution, reciprocity, proximity, vote-buying/canvassing indices after the election; 2016/2021 election outcomes; 2016–17 PLE scores. Several coding details and missing-component rules NR.

evidence.anchor: Treatmentvp is an indicator for assignment to the intervention
evidence.paraphrase: Equation (1) defines treatment, spillover, eligibility, and ACFIM-presence variables; pure-control observations are the comparison. Several indices are described, but not every component's full coding/missing-component rule.

evidence.anchor: The surveys started on March 2, 2016, and ended on July 19, 2016
evidence.paraphrase: The intervention occurred in Uganda during the final three weeks before the February 2016 election; endline survey dates were March 2–July 19, 2016.

evidence.anchor: we can assign test scores to 2,052 polling stations in 695 parishes
evidence.paraphrase: Test scores were matched for 2,052 polling stations; footnote 12 identifies spatial-data and score-data losses.

design_map.label: Estimand
design_map.value: ITT direct-treatment effect α1, spillover effect α2, and average linear saturation effect γ1.

evidence.anchor: We focus on the treatment and spillover estimates, α1 and α2
evidence.paraphrase: Equation (1) defines ITT direct-treatment and spillover coefficients; equation (2) defines γ1 as the average effect of randomized saturation across treatment and spillover villages.

design_map.label: Estimator or statistical model
design_map.value: Linear regression equations (1) and (2) displayed; fitting estimator and weighting rule NR.

evidence.anchor: Our baseline, pre-specified equation is the following intent-to-treat (ITT) specification
evidence.paraphrase: The article prints both regression specifications and identifies their coefficient interpretations, but does not explicitly name the fitting estimator (for example, OLS) or state a weighting rule.

design_map.label: Analysis unit
design_map.value: Voter for survey regressions; polling station for electoral and matched-school analyses.

evidence.anchor: regressions conducted using the survey data are estimated at the voter level
evidence.paraphrase: Survey analyses use voters; electoral analyses use polling stations. Table 6 uses polling-station observations matched to the closest available school.

design_map.label: Variable coding and reference categories
design_map.value: Treatment/spillover/eligibility indicators and pure-control comparator defined; some binary and standardized index outcomes described. Complete component coding/reference/missing rules NR.

evidence.anchor: Treatmentvp is an indicator for assignment to the intervention
evidence.paraphrase: Equation (1) defines treatment, spillover, eligibility, and ACFIM-presence variables; pure-control observations are the comparison. Several indices are described, but not every component's full coding/missing-component rule.

design_map.label: Covariates and fixed effects
design_map.value: Eligibility indicator, parish ACFIM presence, listed individual/electoral controls; 2015 test score in Table 6 cols. 5–6. Baseline fixed-effects and weights NR; strata FE appear only as a robustness change.

evidence.anchor: These controls include, from the survey data, the age, years of education, and marital status
evidence.paraphrase: Footnote 13 lists survey and electoral covariates; equations include eligibility and ACFIM presence. Tables identify baseline-score adjustment. No baseline weighting rule is reported.

evidence.anchor: including a 4th order polynomial ... deciles ... strata fixed effects
evidence.paraphrase: The main text explains the alternative control functions, strata fixed effects, and minimal-control specification, although numerical robustness results are in the excluded appendix.

design_map.label: Standard-error and inference procedure
design_map.value: Robust SEs clustered by parish; significance stars; Tables 2–5 give sharpened FDR q-values. No CIs or resampling are reported.

evidence.anchor: Robust standard errors clustered by parish are reported in parentheses
evidence.paraphrase: Main result tables use parish-clustered robust standard errors, addressing within-parish repeated observations; Tables 2–5 also show sharpened FDR q-values.
evidence.locator: Table 2 note; same statement in Tables 3–6 notes

evidence.anchor: correction is implemented across all key outcomes in Tables 2 through 5, separately for equations (1) and (2)
evidence.paraphrase: The article identifies sharpened two-stage FDR q-values and their analysis families, and distinguishes the pre-specified equation (1) from the non-pre-specified saturation equation (2). It does not describe the q-value algorithm in the main article.

design_map.label: Handling of clustering or repeated observations
design_map.value: Parish clustering used for survey voters and polling-station observations; this captures within-parish repeated/dependent observations. No separate paired-profile issue.

evidence.anchor: Robust standard errors clustered by parish are reported in parentheses
evidence.paraphrase: Main result tables use parish-clustered robust standard errors, addressing within-parish repeated observations; Tables 2–5 also show sharpened FDR q-values.
evidence.locator: Table 2 note; same statement in Tables 3–6 notes

direct_comparison.summary: Strong visible control quantities and survey-result mapping; incomplete crime-index coding, randomization sequence, covariate identities, administrative-model mapping, RI/CRSE implementation, missingness flow, and SE/CI reporting.
The main article supplies only the diagnostic purpose and a qualitative no-bias conclusion; all reconstructive detail is deferred to the excluded appendix.

findings: Main-text tables, table notes, figure notes, footnotes, and prose were treated as coequal evidence.
Tables 1–5 earned credit for outcome coding, control means, effect estimates, sample sizes, column contrasts, and named p-value procedures wherever their notes made those items explicit.
Credit was not withheld merely because evidence appeared in a table rather than prose.
Appendix pointers were recorded but never treated as evidence for omitted pair construction, spillover models, measurement-diagnostic details, robustness tables, or outcome decompositions.
The same strict standard was applied to the primary and diagnostic randomizations; the diagnostic received zeros where the main article supplied only a qualitative assertion.

execution_record.assessment_scope: Assess the supplied article version using the shared prompt and main-article evidence only. Include primary and embedded list experiments when described in the main article. Classify each design from the supplied article; retain observational designs as unscored inventories under the shared prompt. Exclude online appendices and publisher-added citing-article lists from assessment evidence. Verify and record main-article page boundaries. Source version notes are available in source.json.

experiments.name: Geographic border/distance-shock natural experiment
experiments.classification_rationale: The principal analysis exploits a 1987 comuna-border reorganization and continuous distance shock. The article calls it a natural/quasi-experiment, but reports no randomized sequence or researcher-controlled assignment; under the required taxonomy it is an observational/quasi-experimental analysis and is inventoried without experimental scoring.

classification_evidence.paraphrase: The analysis uses changes in assigned proximity to state headquarters across neighboring blocks rather than a randomized intervention.
Figure 6 explicitly labels blocks near eligible borders as the quasi-experimental sample.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, equations, figures, tables, table notes, and footnotes were treated as equal eligible main-article evidence. Table 1 notes earned credit for WLS adjustment, group-clustered standard errors, inverse-probability weighting, and column interpretation; Table 2 means and estimates earned results credit. No criterion was reduced merely because evidence appeared in a display rather than prose. Appendix pointers were treated only as evidence that information was absent from the main article, never as supplying that information.

direct_comparison.scope: Within-paper comparison of the two focal experiments; cross-paper synthesis is deferred.
direct_comparison.summary: Both focal experiments clearly report ITT OLS, analysis units, clustered robust inference, focal sample sizes, effects, and uncertainty. Phase 1 is more transparent about sequence generation (public lottery), while Phase 2 reports only a computer algorithm. Phase 2 Table 5 is more complete on raw group quantities; Phase 1 Table 3 leaves control quantities blank for two focal IPV/control outcomes. Both omit the exact high-dimensional covariate list, complete outcome/index coding, multiplicity handling, and reconstructable robustness specifications.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, tables, figures, table notes, and figure notes were given equal evidentiary status. Table 3 and Table 5 notes earned credit for OLS, comparator, subgroups, fixed effects, clustered robust SEs, CIs, and samples. Figure 1 earned participant-flow and stratification credit. No score was reduced merely because evidence appeared in a display rather than prose. Conversely, appendix pointers did not supply omitted covariates, robustness specifications, or outcome construction.

checks.detail: Table and note evidence was used directly for criteria 5–8, 11, and 14–17.
Figure 1 supplied flow/strata; Figure 2 supplied standardization and CI basis.
Weights, exact covariates, computer sequence generation, missing-outcome rules, multiplicity, and robustness details were scored absent when not stated.
Online Appendix A/B/C and Blattman et al. references were not treated as evidence.

execution_record.assessment_scope: Assess the supplied article version using the shared prompt and main-article evidence only. Include primary and embedded list experiments when described in the main article. Classify each design from the supplied article; retain observational designs as unscored inventories under the shared prompt. Exclude online appendices and publisher-added citing-article lists from assessment evidence. Verify and record main-article page boundaries. Source version notes are available in source.json.

title: Generating Skilled Self-Employment in Developing Countries: Experimental Evidence from Uganda

direct_comparison.scope: Single-paper independent session; comparisons are across experiment classes within this article, not across papers.
findings: The primary experiment is the most statistically traceable: Tables 2–8 report outcomes, estimates, clustered SEs, control means, covariates, and sample sizes.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, tables, table notes, footnotes, and figure notes were given equal evidentiary status. Full credit was awarded where they jointly resolved a component (notably Tables 2–8 and 10); no credit was given to appendix pointers or inferred customary practice.

execution_record.assessment_scope: Assess the supplied article version using the shared prompt and main-article evidence only. title: Does alleviating poverty increase cognitive performance? Short- and long-term evidence from a randomized controlled trial

reviewed_pages.main_article_boundary: PDF pages 1–32; title page 1, article text 2–28, references 28–31, blank manuscript page 32. No embedded appendix or publisher-added citing-article list.
reviewed_pages.scoring_evidence_pages: PDF pages 4–27, especially Figures 1–6; pages 1–32 reviewed for boundaries and inventory.

source_scope: Supplied published main-article PDF only, including main-text figures, notes, and footnotes. External articles, the linked Stage 1 protocol, OSF materials, appendix, code, and prior publication are excluded as evidence.
inventory_notes: One distinct randomized experiment was identified and scored as primary (category 1).
The therapy and cash assignments are sequential factors in the same four-cell trial, not separate randomized samples.
The 100-person first implementation phase was pooled into the trial and is not a separate pilot experiment.
No category 2 or 3 experiment, embedded list experiment, category 4 pilot with no outcome, or category 5 observational analysis was identified.
The BF design simulations and literature mini-meta-analysis are analysis/planning procedures, not experiments conducted on a new randomized sample in this article.

findings: Tables and table notes received the same evidentiary status as prose.
Table 3 earned evidence credit for n=1,025, estimators, block dummies, baseline covariates, village clustering, effects, and standard errors.
Tables 4, 6, and 7 received credit for their displayed outcomes, control means, estimates, uncertainty, model labels, and clustering notes, but not for sample sizes they do not display.
Appendix pointers were recorded as pointers and did not supply omitted index components, robustness methods, or results.
Absence judgments were based on review of all PDF pages 1–17 and the relevant displays; no quotation was invented to establish absence.
